blocks.body:
There are two quite different ways to say that a statement $\varphi$ follows from assumptions $\Gamma$. The semantic way: $\varphi$ is true in every structure in which all of $\Gamma$ is true, written $\Gamma \models \varphi$. This quantifies over all structures, infinitely many of them, of every size. The syntactic way: there is a proof, a finite list of formulas, each an assumption, an axiom, or obtained from earlier ones by a fixed rule, ending in $\varphi$; written $\Gamma \vdash \varphi$. This is a finite, mechanical object that a computer could check.

Gödel's completeness theorem (proved in his 1929 dissertation, published 1930) says the two notions agree for first-order logic: a sentence follows from $\Gamma$ in every possible world exactly when it can be formally proved from $\Gamma$. Its most useful consequence, the compactness theorem, turns this into a powerful construction tool: to build a structure with infinitely many required properties, it is enough to satisfy any finitely many of them at a time.

blocks.title: Setting: structures and consequence
blocks.body:
We use the first-order languages of [[logic-basics]]: a language has constant, function and relation symbols; formulas are built from atomic formulas with $\neg$, $\to$ and $\forall$ (the other connectives and $\exists$ being abbreviations); a sentence has no free variables. A structure $\mathfrak A$ gives a nonempty domain and interprets each symbol. A model of a set of sentences $\Gamma$ is a structure in which every sentence of $\Gamma$ is true. Then $\Gamma \models \varphi$ means every model of $\Gamma$ is a model of $\varphi$, and $\Gamma$ is satisfiable if it has a model.

For example, let $\Gamma$ be the axioms for groups in a language with a binary symbol $\cdot$, a constant $e$ and a unary symbol ${}^{-1}$. Then $\Gamma \models \forall x\, \forall y\, \forall z\, (x \cdot y = x \cdot z \to y = z)$, since cancellation holds in every group. But $\Gamma \not\models \forall x\, \forall y\, (x \cdot y = y \cdot x)$: the symmetric group $S_3$ is a model of $\Gamma$ in which this sentence is false. A single countermodel is how non-consequence is shown.

blocks.title: A deductive calculus

blocks.body: By [[induction]] on the length of the deduction, show that every formula in it is true in every model of $\Gamma$ under every assignment of values to its free variables. Members of $\Gamma$ are true by assumption. Each logical axiom is true in every structure; for scheme 1 because tautologies are true whatever truth values their parts take, and for schemes 2 to 5 by short checks from the definition of truth (scheme 2 needs the substitution lemma, which says that $\alpha^x_t$ holds under an assignment exactly when $\alpha$ holds after giving $x$ the value of $t$). Finally, if $\alpha$ and $\alpha \to \beta$ are both true under an assignment, so is $\beta$.

blocks.title: Gödel's completeness theorem
blocks.body: If $\Gamma \models \varphi$, then $\Gamma \vdash \varphi$. Equivalently: every consistent set of sentences has a model.

blocks.title: Proof sketch (Henkin's method, countable language)
blocks.body:
First, the second form implies the first (the converse is similar and not needed). If $\Gamma \models \varphi$ then $\Gamma \cup \{
eg\varphi\}$ has no model; if every consistent set has a model, $\Gamma \cup \{
eg\varphi\}$ must be inconsistent, so it proves $\varphi$, and by the deduction theorem $\Gamma \vdash 
eg\varphi 	o \varphi$, from which $\Gamma \vdash \varphi$ by a tautology.

Now let $\Gamma$ be consistent. The idea is to build a model out of the language itself.

1. Witnesses. Add infinitely many new constants. List all formulas $	heta_1(x), 	heta_2(x), \dots$ of the enlarged language with one free variable, and for each add the Henkin axiom $
eg  orall x\, 	heta_n(x) 	o 
eg 	heta_n(c_n)$, with $c_n$ a new constant not occurring in $	heta_1, \dots, 	heta_n$ or in the earlier Henkin axioms. Intuitively: if something fails $	heta_n$, then $c_n$ names such a thing. One shows the enlarged set is still consistent.
2. Maximality. List all sentences $\sigma_1, \sigma_2, \dots$ and go through them, adding $\sigma_k$ if that keeps the set consistent and $
eg\sigma_k$ otherwise (Lindenbaum's lemma). The result $\Delta$ is consistent and, for each sentence $\sigma$, contains exactly one of $\sigma$ and $
eg\sigma$.
3. The term model. Let the domain be the closed terms, with $t$ and $u$ identified when the sentence $t = u$ is in $\Delta$ (the equality axioms make this an equivalence relation compatible with all symbols). Interpret each constant as (the class of) itself, each function symbol $f$ by sending the classes of $t_1, \dots, t_n$ to the class of $f(t_1,\dots,t_n)$, and each relation symbol $R$ by declaring $R(t_1,\dots,t_n)$ true exactly when that sentence is in $\Delta$.
4. Truth lemma. By induction on formulas, a sentence is true in the term model if and only if it is in $\Delta$. The atomic case is the definition; $
eg$ and $	o$ use maximality; and $ orall$ is where the witnesses are needed: if $ orall x\, 	heta(x) 
otin \Delta$, then the witness $c$ satisfies $
eg	heta(c) \in \Delta$, so $ orall x\, 	heta(x)$ fails in the model too.

Since $\Gamma \subseteq \Delta$, the term model (restricted to the original language) is a model of $\Gamma$. Note that its domain is countable, a fact used below.

blocks.title: Compactness theorem
blocks.body: A set of sentences $\Gamma$ has a model if and only if every finite subset of $\Gamma$ has a model. Equivalently, if $\Gamma \models \varphi$ then $\Gamma_0 \models \varphi$ for some finite $\Gamma_0 \subseteq \Gamma$.

One direction is trivial. For the other, suppose $\Gamma$ has no model. By completeness $\Gamma$ is inconsistent, so it proves some $\psi$ and $\neg \psi$. The two deductions are finite lists, so together they use only finitely many members of $\Gamma$; call this finite set $\Gamma_0$. Then $\Gamma_0$ is inconsistent, and by soundness it has no model.

blocks.title: What compactness buys
blocks.body:
Stated this way, compactness mentions only models, not proofs. Typical uses:

Arbitrarily large finite models force infinite ones. If $\Gamma$ has finite models of every size, add the sentences $\lambda_n$: "there are at least $n$ elements", that is $\exists x_1 \cdots \exists x_n \bigwedge_{i<j} x_i \ne x_j$. Each finite subset of $\Gamma \cup \{\lambda_2, \lambda_3, \dots\}$ has a model, so the whole set does, and that model is infinite. Consequently no set of first-order sentences has exactly the finite groups (or finite fields, or finite graphs) as its models.

Nonstandard arithmetic. Let $\mathrm{Th}(\mathbb N)$ be all sentences true in $(\mathbb N, 0, S, +, \cdot, <)$. Add a constant $c$ and the sentences $c > \underline{n}$ for each $n$, where $\underline{n}$ is $S S \cdots S 0$. Any finite subset is true in $\mathbb N$ if $c$ is interpreted as a large enough number, so there is a model of everything true about $\mathbb N$ that also contains an element larger than every standard number. Such a model satisfies exactly the same first-order sentences as $\mathbb N$, so "being a standard natural number" is not first-order expressible. The same trick applied to $\mathbb R$ produces fields with infinitesimals, the starting point of Robinson's nonstandard analysis.

Löwenheim–Skolem. The Henkin model above is countable, so every consistent set of sentences in a countable language has a countable model. Even axioms for set theory, which prove that uncountable sets exist, have countable models (Skolem's paradox: "uncountable" inside the model only means that the model contains no bijection with its own $\omega$).

blocks.title: A formal deduction
blocks.body: Using only scheme 1 instances and modus ponens, give a deduction of $p \to p$ (for a fixed formula $p$) that uses the tautologies $\alpha \to (\beta \to \alpha)$ and $(\alpha \to (\beta \to \gamma)) \to ((\alpha \to \beta) \to (\alpha \to \gamma))$.
blocks.solution:
Of course $p \to p$ is itself a tautology, so in this calculus it is an axiom. The point of the exercise is to see how the two schemes, which also form the core of the classic Hilbert systems, generate it.

1. $(p \to ((p \to p) \to p)) \to ((p \to (p \to p)) \to (p \to p))$, the second scheme with $\alpha = p$, $\beta = p \to p$, $\gamma = p$.
2. $p \to ((p \to p) \to p)$, the first scheme with $\alpha = p$, $\beta = p \to p$.
3. $(p \to (p \to p)) \to (p \to p)$, modus ponens from 2 and 1.
4. $p \to (p \to p)$, the first scheme with $\alpha = \beta = p$.
5. $p \to p$, modus ponens from 4 and 3.

blocks.title: Non-consequence by countermodel
blocks.body: Show that $\forall x\, \exists y\, R(x,y) \not\vdash \exists y\, \forall x\, R(x,y)$.
blocks.solution:
By soundness it is enough to find a structure where the hypothesis is true and the conclusion is false. Take the domain $\{0, 1\}$ and let $R(x,y)$ mean $x \ne y$. Every $x$ has a $y$ different from it, so $\forall x\, \exists y\, R(x,y)$ holds. But no $y$ is different from every $x$, since $y$ is not different from itself. So $\exists y\, \forall x\, R(x,y)$ is false.

Completeness gives the converse: whenever no countermodel exists, a deduction does. This turns "is it provable?" into "is there a counterexample?", and vice versa.

blocks.title: Connectedness is not first-order
blocks.body: In the language with one binary relation symbol $E$ (edges of a graph), show that there is no set $\Gamma$ of sentences whose models are exactly the connected graphs.
blocks.solution:
Suppose such a $\Gamma$ existed. Add two constants $a, b$, and for each $n \ge 1$ the sentence $\delta_n$: "there is no path of length at most $n$ from $a$ to $b$". For instance $\delta_2$ is
$$a 
e b \wedge 
eg E(a,b) \wedge 
eg \exists z\,  ig(E(a,z) \wedge E(z,b) ig).$$
Take any finite subset of $\Gamma \cup \{\delta_1, \delta_2, \dots\}$, and let $N$ be the largest $n$ for which $\delta_n$ occurs. A path with $N + 2$ vertices, with $a$ and $b$ its two ends, is connected (so it satisfies $\Gamma$), and its ends are at distance $N + 1$, so it satisfies $\delta_1, \dots, \delta_N$. By compactness the whole set has a model: a graph satisfying $\Gamma$, hence connected, in which $a$ and $b$ are joined by no path of any length. This is a contradiction.

blocks.title: Colouring infinite graphs
blocks.body: Let $G$ be a graph with countably many vertices such that every finite subgraph can be properly coloured with 3 colours. Prove that $G$ itself can be properly 3-coloured.

- Completeness is not the same as the completeness of a theory. Gödel's completeness theorem is about the logic: every valid consequence is provable. A theory $T$ is called complete if it proves $\sigma$ or $\neg\sigma$ for every sentence $\sigma$; the [[incompleteness]] theorems say arithmetic is not complete in this second sense. The two results do not conflict.
- Completeness does not give a decision procedure. Provable consequences can be listed one by one, but if $\varphi$ is not a consequence, the search may never end; first-order validity is undecidable (Church and Turing).
- Compactness fails for stronger logics. In second-order logic one can characterise $\mathbb N$ up to isomorphism, so the nonstandard-model argument breaks down, and so does completeness.
- In the compactness argument, each finite subset may need a different model; there is no claim that one model of a finite subset extends to a model of everything.

The completeness theorem is the base camp for [[incompleteness]]: once provability in first-order logic is known to capture truth in all models, Gödel's second great result shows that no reasonable axiom system captures truth in the one intended model $\mathbb N$. Compactness and Löwenheim–Skolem are the opening theorems of model theory, and the countable models they produce connect to [[ordinals-cardinals]]. The propositional form of compactness is the logical core of results in [[infinite-combinatorics]], such as infinite colouring theorems, and the undecidability of validity is a theorem of [[computability]].

1. Show that $$\{\forall x\, \neg R(x,x),\ \forall x\, \forall y\, \forall z\, (R(x,y) \wedge R(y,z) \to R(x,z))\} \not\models \forall x\, \forall y\, (R(x,y) \vee x = y \vee R(y,x))$$.
2. Use compactness to show that if a sentence is true in every field of characteristic 0, then it is true in every field of characteristic $p$ for all sufficiently large primes $p$.
3. Prove that there is no set of sentences in the language of ordered sets whose models are exactly the well-orders. (Hint: add constants $c_0 > c_1 > c_2 > \cdots$.)
